Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00806

The Illuminationist author, Suhrawardi, says that knowledge is appearance, and that appearance is the very reality of light. Light may shine by itself, or it may shine on something else. If it shines by itself, it is aware of itself. If it shines on something else, that other thing may or may not shine by itself. If it does not, it may be dark in itself, or it may shine on something else, or it may not shine at all but be darkness for something else. In the first case, that other thing perceives the light. In the other three cases, it does not perceive the light and is not aware of itself. This is the core of Suhrawardi's view: a thing knows itself by being light to itself, and knows something else through a relation of light between two things that are both light.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00807

These accounts seem to contradict one another. But they can be understood as different ways of describing one view: knowledge is an existence free of matter, an existence from which material coverings have been removed.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00808

If this free existence belongs to itself, it understands itself. If it belongs to something else, as in the case of physical qualities, it understands that other thing—or imagines or senses it. This is the general meaning of knowledge. We will now challenge what the different accounts seem to say, build the view we take to be true, and then, as far as possible, show how the other accounts can be understood in line with it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00809

First, the claim that understanding is something negative is plainly false. When we look inward while understanding something, we find that something has come to be present to us; we do not find that something has simply gone away. Also, if knowledge were a kind of absence, it would have to be the absence of something in particular. The most obvious thing for it to be the absence of is its opposite, ignorance. Ignorance can be simple or confused. Simple ignorance is simply not knowing something. If knowledge were the absence of this ignorance, it would mean not not-knowing, which is the positive presence of knowledge. So knowledge would be positive, not negative. If it were the absence of confused ignorance, there would be a middle state between knowing and not knowing, because the absence of confused ignorance does not necessarily give us knowledge. So knowledge cannot be the absence of confused ignorance either.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00810

Confused ignorance combines knowledge and ignorance. If knowledge were its absence, that absence would either cancel the knowledge within it, which would mean knowledge cancels itself, or cancel the ignorance within it, which brings us back to the first case: knowledge as the absence of ignorance. Someone might reply that knowledge does not mean the absence of ignorance; it means freedom from matter and its features. This is wrong for three reasons. First, freedom from matter is not true of one person but not another. We would not say that the sun is free of matter in relation to Zayd but not in relation to Amr, as we say that Zayd understands something and Amr does not. If knowing something meant that it was free of matter, then instead of saying “Zayd knows that the world began,” we could say “Zayd is free of matter in the claim that the world began.” That is not what we mean.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00811

Second, knowing that something has no position or direction is not the same as knowing something. If knowing meant exactly the same as being free of matter, then whenever we knew that something was immaterial, we would also know it as an object of knowledge. But we do not. Someone may know that a thing is immaterial and still doubt whether it understands anything, or understands itself. A proof is needed to establish that every immaterial thing is an intellect, understands itself, or understands something else. One meaning cannot be both unknown and known at the same time. Third, as we said, when we know something we find a positive state within ourselves, distinct from other states of the soul such as wanting, choosing, fear, desire, or anger. So perceiving something is not simply an absence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00812

The second account says that knowledge is an image imprinted in the knower. This also fails, for three reasons. First, if understanding were the presence of an image within the knower, we could not understand ourselves. But we know from our own experience that we do. So the argument fails. For us to understand ourselves, either that understanding would have to be our very self, or another image of our self would have to exist within us. Neither answer works. If understanding ourselves were simply our self, then anyone who knew their self would also know that they understand their self. And anyone who understood something that understands itself would know that it understands itself—and would understand its understanding of itself. But that is not what happens.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00813

The second answer also fails. The image of our self would have to be like our self. That would mean two identical things together, or one thing existing in another when there is no reason to treat one as the container and the other as what it contains. It would also mean that one thing was both a substance and an accident. Our self is a substance that does not depend on something else to exist. But something that exists in a substance after that substance is already present is an accident. Finally, every mental image is general, even if we add a thousand details to it: it can still apply to more than one thing. But we know our self as one particular being that cannot be shared. Anything added to the self can be pointed to as “that”; we point to the self itself as “I.” So knowledge of the self cannot be an extra image of the self.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00814

The second reason the image account fails is that lifeless bodies are also joined to forms, but do not perceive them. So the form's mere presence in a thing cannot be what makes that thing aware of it. If someone replies that knowledge is the presence of an image in something capable of understanding, this defines knowledge by knowledge itself. Our senses receive images too, yet images are not all received in the same way. We sense an object by means of an image from it, and we sense several things together, even when those things have opposites.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00815

The answer that knowledge is the presence of an image free of matter in an immaterial thing also fails. Understanding is a positive state, while freedom from matter is a negative idea. A negative idea cannot be part of the very nature of something positive, such as understanding. So either understanding is simply the presence of the thing, which we have already rejected, or it is another positive state that occurs when the image is free of matter. We will return to this difficult point and show how the account is true in one sense and false in another. In any case, it amounts to admitting that perception is not just the presence of an image.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00816
The third account says that knowledge is a relation between the knower and the known, with no further state in the knower.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00817

This is also wrong. As we explained when discussing relations, a relation cannot exist on its own; it exists only when the two things it connects exist. Yet we often understand things that have no existence outside the mind. We also understand ourselves, though a relation between us and ourselves exists only as something we think about. If knowledge were only a relation, we would not know anything unless we first thought of the relation and compared the two sides. But we are always aware of ourselves, whether or not we think about this relation. People who say knowledge is a relation take this view to avoid some problems with treating knowledge as an image, but they overlook that a relation requires both things to exist. Their account would make nonexistent things impossible to know. It would also make all knowledge true, because they take ignorance to mean that a mental image does not match a real thing outside us.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00818

The fourth account, chosen by the author of Al-Mulakhkhaṣ, says that knowledge is a quality in the soul that is also related to an outside thing. This view is deeply flawed. First, it would mean that God's knowledge of Himself and of other things is a quality added to His own being. God is one and self-sufficient, so His perfect attributes cannot be the weakest kind of created feature. If knowledge were a quality added to God, God would have existed before that quality and would not yet have known anything. Nor could this quality itself be necessary in itself, since that would mean there was more than one Necessary Being. Then God's knowledge of things would come from something possible and dependent on Him. But the source of all perfection cannot receive perfection from something else.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00819

Also, proof shows that our knowledge of ourselves is not separate from ourselves. If knowledge were a quality, our self would be a quality too, even though it is a substance. In imagination we see high mountains, wide deserts, the sky, and the earth. These are substances, so our knowledge of them cannot consist only of qualities. Anyone who says that every mental image is a quality has no proof for this. If they say that the images are not enough and another quality must be present as well, they must prove it. Suhrawardi's view, by contrast, contains some truth and some error. He is right that when a separate substance knows itself, its knowledge consists in being light to itself; light is existence. This brings us back to our view that knowledge is existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00820

What is wrong in his account is that he treats knowing something other than oneself as a relation to it. This cannot be right, since knowledge divides into concepts and judgments, general and particular knowledge, while a relation is not divided in those ways. It would also mean that every animal, which has particular forms of awareness, has intellect, since Suhrawardi says that anything aware of something must be light to itself. And according to his view, bodies and sizes can know through this direct presence. He also says that every one of us knows their body directly in this way. We hold that physical bodies, as they exist in matter and extend in different directions, are not aware of anything.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00821

Our chosen view—that knowledge is existence free of matter and position—also seems to face many objections, but they can all be answered with careful thought. One objection says that a mental image must either match the outside thing, in which case some outside thing must exist for it to match, or fail to match, in which case it is ignorance. How, then, could perception be only a relation between the perceiver and the thing perceived? This was raised by an early commentator on The Pointers. Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi replied that some images match what is outside the mind, and these are knowledge; others do not, and these are ignorance. A relation itself cannot match or fail to match something outside the mind, because it cannot exist there.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00822

I say that the objector's words suggest that an image that does not match the outside world is ignorance in the sense of having no knowledge at all—not ignorance as a false belief, which is itself a kind of knowledge. The word “knowledge” and the word “ignorance” each have two meanings here. Otherwise, the objection has no force. In fact, it supports the view that knowledge is the image itself. When a false image exists in the mind, it is certainly one kind of knowledge, even though it does not match anything outside the mind. There is no relation connecting it to an outside thing. So knowledge can exist without such a relation.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00823

A second objection says that an image is needed only when the thing does not exist outside the mind; when it does exist, knowledge might simply be a relation to it. The reply is that perception and knowledge name the same general reality, whether it appears as understanding, imagining, or sensing. If this reality is an image in some cases, with a relation added to it, then it cannot be a relation in other cases.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00824

Another objection says that if perceiving black were simply having black present in something, then a black body would perceive black. The answer is that not every kind of presence is perception. The image must be present in a way free from matter and position.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00825

A third objection says that if perceiving means having an image that is free of matter, then whenever we know that a thing exists independently, we should know that it understands. And once we know that God is neither a body nor material, we should not need a separate proof to know whether He knows Himself or whether His knowledge is identical with His own being.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00826

I say that knowledge is not the general idea of an image free from matter. If that were all it meant, then merely thinking about this idea would make us sure that a thing knows. Rather, knowledge is an actual existence free from matter. We cannot grasp an existence in its full reality through a mental picture; we know it through its own actual presence. If such an existence were present to our intellect, we would know without doubt that it understands itself and what is present to it. No proof would be needed.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00827

A fourth objection concerns knowing ourselves. If understanding ourselves is simply our self, then our knowledge that we know ourselves must also be the self. And if that knowledge is the same as our knowledge of ourselves, it too must be the self. This would continue without end and create an endless chain of mental combinations. But if knowing that we know ourselves is not the same as knowing ourselves, then it seems that knowing ourselves cannot be the self either.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00828

Al-Tusi, in his commentary on The Aims of the Pointers, reports this objection from al-Masʿūdī. He answers that knowledge of ourselves is our self in one sense, but not in another: the mind can consider one thing in many ways.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00829

I say that answer does not remove the problem. A better answer is this: our direct awareness of ourselves is the very existence of our self. But our idea that we are aware of ourselves is not that existence. It is another mental image, different from our particular self. Our knowledge of that knowledge is yet another image, and so on, until we stop considering it. This does not mean that two identical images exist at the same level. As we have said many times, existence—whether in the outside world or in the mind—has no copy or image that matches it in its own identity. When we know our particular existence through an added idea, that idea is an accident that exists in us, but it is different from our existence and is not its copy. The same applies to knowledge of any kind. Each kind of knowledge is a way of existing. We know an existence only through its own presence, not through another image of it. So we can know an existence as a particular only in a general way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00830

Another objection says that when we see something, the thing we see is Zayd himself, who exists outside us. To say we see only his copy or likeness, they say, would make us doubt the most obvious things. The commentator answers that what we see is Zayd; the act of seeing is the presence of his likeness in the sense organ. Confusing the thing seen with the act of seeing caused the objection.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00831

I say the truth is this: the true object of sight is an imaginal individual that exists in the outside world, but not in the eye itself. I will explain this further in its place, if God wills. That is a brief outline of the views philosophers have held about knowledge and the problems with each. Now I will set out more fully the view I have been pointing to.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00832
IV. What Knowledge Really Is
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00833

Knowledge is not something negative, like being free of matter. Nor is it a relation. It is existence—but not every kind of existence. It is actual existence, not potential existence; and not all actual existence, but existence free of nonexistence. The more free of nonexistence an existence is, the stronger its being knowledge.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00834

Here is why. First matter is unclear in itself and does not exist in a complete, actual way. It becomes a definite thing only when it takes on a body and the features that come with a body, such as motion. A body, simply as a body, does not have existence that is free of nonexistence. If we imagine one part of it existing, the other parts and the whole are absent. If that part exists, the whole is not there; and the other parts are absent too. Existence is either the same as unity or bound up with it. What has no unity has no existence. Likewise, predication and being one and the same depend on unity. What cannot be one with anything has no existence at all. No part of a continuous body, even one we mark off in thought, can be said of the whole; and the whole cannot be said of any one of its parts. Yet the body's identity comes from its parts being joined, and it becomes more complete as that connection continues. But how could a thing's completion bring about its disappearance?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00835

In short, a body is a reality that separates itself as it exists, and carries the possibility of its own nonexistence. Its existence and the existence of one part—say, a forearm—are the nonexistence of another part or of another body. So a body always carries the possibility of its own passing away. This is existence at its weakest: a thing exists in a way that brings about its own absence. This is like the relation between many things and unity. A group is one, but its unity consists in there being many members.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00836

First matter is weak in a different way: it is pure potential to become many things. A body, by contrast, exists in a way that contains the potential for its own absence. Such a thing is never fully present to itself. And if it is not fully present to itself, nothing else can fully grasp it either. Knowing and perceiving require this full presence. So no one knows a body or its changing features through the body's material image itself. We know it only through another kind of image, not the material, spatial image outside us. That material image cannot exist in something else without being in its material setting or being involved with what is in that setting. The same goes for the material form of a body: it has no existence on its own. Each thing exists only at its own edges and limits, and its edge is outside what it is. But understanding reaches a thing itself and the parts that belong within it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00837

What we have said shows that existence by itself is not enough for something to perceive or be perceived. It must be an existence without bodily position and direction, which are features of a category of material things. Actual existence, free of these absences, is perception. This may be what earlier writers meant by the further state that occurs alongside the presence of an image: a stronger and more independent existence, not divided into parts and not located in any one region of the material world. Every image that gives us knowledge has this kind of existence. A mental image is not something we can point to in space. What the senses directly perceive is not, in truth, the same as the material qualities called heat or cold, the first things we touch. These qualities are sensed only indirectly. What is directly sensed is an image whose existence is the same as its being sensed. As we have explained, the existence of what is understood and its being understood are one. The directly sensed image is not in a spatial position, although the sense organ and the outside object must be related in space for the image to arise. This spatial relation is not needed for imagination, inner thought, or reason. Nor is the image present in the mind in the same way as an image exists in physical matter. We will explain the differences between these two kinds of presence next.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00838
V. How a Mental Image Is Present to the Soul but Exists Differently in Matter
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00839

There are eight differences. First, material qualities crowd each other out. Something with one shape or color cannot have a different shape or color at the same time. The same is true of conflicting tastes, smells, and sounds. But mental images do not crowd each other out. The power that brings our senses together can take them all in at once. Each of the five senses can also perceive different kinds within its field: sight sees opposite colors, taste senses opposite flavors, and so on. So an image in perception has a different kind of existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00840

Second, a large thing cannot exist in a small material thing. A mountain cannot fit in a mustard seed, and an ocean cannot fit in a pond. This is different in perception: the soul receives large and small things alike. It can hold the image of all the heavens and the earth and everything between them at once, without becoming cramped. As our master and leader Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, is reported to have said, “The heart of the believer is greater than the Throne.” Abū Yazīd al-Basṭāmī is also reported to have said, “If the Throne and all it contains were in one corner of Abū Yazīd’s heart, he would not even notice.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00841

The reason is that the soul has no size or position. If it did, it would have fixed limits and could not take in anything larger or smaller than those limits. Some part of the thing would then escape it, or some part of the soul would fail to grasp what it received. One thing would be both known and unknown, or both knowing and not knowing, at the same time. This is impossible, both by reason and by experience. We know that the soul is one. When it perceives something large, it perceives all of it with its whole self, not with a part, since it has no parts.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00842

Third, a weak quality in matter disappears when a stronger one arrives. But mental images remain together. A strong image does not erase a weaker one, especially in imagination and thought. The intellect can remember a faint effect after a stronger one, and can picture something small after something large, or something weaker after something more intense.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00843

Fourth, material qualities can be pointed to by the senses and occupy a place in the world. Mental images cannot be pointed to or located in space. Fifth, one material image can be perceived by many people: many people can read the same writing or hear the same sound. A mental image cannot be shared in this way. No one else can look into what is in my imagination, or taste what I taste. That is why people say that the fire in the soul does not burn, a lover’s burning heart does not heat anything, and the ice in their chest does not cool anything.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00844

When the intellect says that fire burns and water cools, it does not mean that the images in the mind burn or cool. It means that things outside the mind do so. Likewise, when we say that a substance exists on its own and does not depend on something else, we are speaking of the thing represented in the mind, not the mental image itself. The image in the mind can depend on the mind that holds it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00845

Sixth, when a material image disappears from its subject, it cannot be restored—or replaced by the same kind of image—without new learning or a new cause. A mental image, by contrast, can often be brought back once we have formed it, without having to learn it all over again. Seventh, when a material thing is incomplete, it needs a separate cause to complete it. A tree needs water and soil to grow. An animal needs other causes to reach full growth. The same is true of natural and made things: they need causes outside themselves to complete what is missing. But images in the soul, such as the images in a soul that has received divine support, can begin incomplete and reach the perfection suited to them through their own resources, without a separate being completing them.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00846

Eighth, the opposite of a material thing cannot be truly said of it. Outside the mind, fire is fire, not nonfire; blackness is blackness, not nonblackness. But mental fire is not fire in the ordinary, concrete sense; a mental body is not a body in that sense. The same is true of colors, sounds, tastes, and smells. We can say of them both that they are what they mean and that they are not what they mean, depending on how we use the words: in one sense, the mental image is fire; in another, it is not. This is the key to understanding the point, and how one image can be described in opposite ways without contradiction.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00847

The reason is that this kind of image, stripped of material limits, has a higher and more complete existence. When we affirm that it has material features, we mean that the source and root of those features are present in it. Material images are like molded figures of the more complete images. We deny those material features because the more complete images are too high and noble to exist in this lower material form. This flesh-and-blood animal, made of opposing elements and constantly changing forms, is an image and shadow of the simpler animal in the soul. Above it stands the intellectual animal: one simple reality that gathers within itself all the material and mental members of its kind. Thus there is an intellectual horse, the general model of horses. The same is true of other animals and other kinds of things, as we explained when discussing essences.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00848

The point here is to show how mental images that match material things can also be described in ways that seem opposite to their material forms, without contradiction. This depends on understanding how something can grow stronger or weaker in existence. When existence becomes stronger, a thing can rise out of its earlier kind into a higher kind, even though it becomes more fully what it was. As the common saying goes, once something passes its limit, it turns into its opposite. The same happens when one material being develops: an embryo first takes on a natural form, then a soul, and then intellect. What it could not be said to have earlier can now be said of it, while features that were true of it before may no longer apply.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00849
VI. On the Claim That Knowledge Is an Accident
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00850

In our view, images formed through the senses or imagination do not exist as accidents in the sense organs. The organs are like mirrors and places where these images appear, not the things that contain them. The images themselves are immaterial substances, while their qualities are features of those substances. All of them exist in the soul, as possible things exist through God.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00851

As for intellectual knowledge, the common view is that we know things because their images are imprinted in our souls. Knowledge is then an image of an existing thing, stripped of its matter. It may be the image of a substance or of a quality. But this raises a serious problem, described by Avicenna in The Healing: knowledge must match what is known. If the thing known is a substance that exists on its own, then knowledge of it must match that substance and belong to the same kind. Whatever belongs to the same kind as a substance must fall under the same broad category. But substance is a category said of the things beneath it. So the mind’s image of a substance must itself be a substance. Yet knowledge is usually called a quality of the soul, an accident that exists in the soul. The same thing would then be both a substance and an accident, though nothing that is a substance is an accident. This is the well-known problem. We have already indicated how to answer it, and will return to it later. Avicenna’s answer is that the nature of a substance is to exist outside the mind without depending on a subject. The same description applies to the essence of a substance as the mind understands it: it is an essence that, if it existed outside the mind, would not depend on a subject. In the mind, however, it does not exist in that way. Motion is similar: its nature is to be the completion of something that exists potentially, but motion in the mind is not itself a completion of something in that way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00852

I say that this answer does not satisfy me. If the arguments for mental existence are sound, they show that things exist in the mind with all their features, relations, and meanings, but in a different way from their fading, material existence. We imagine a human being not only as a kind of substance but also as something that exists on its own, understands itself, and does not depend on a subject. Avicenna’s answer cannot explain this. If we applied it to every feature, broader kind, and distinguishing feature of an essence, nothing of the essence would remain in the mind. If the image of an animal in the mind were not a substance, body, living thing, perceiver, mover, or anything else that belongs to an animal, what would make it an animal? Would it be an animal because it is an actual bodily substance that lives, senses, and moves? No. Or would it be an animal because, if it existed outside the mind, it would be an animal?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00853

What could that last claim mean? If it means that this very mental image, as one individual, could exist outside the mind, that is false. The individual in the mind has become general and can apply to many things; it cannot leave the mind and become that very bodily individual with a particular position and direction. That would confuse different kinds of existence and erase their differences. An individual in the mind can be general and apply to many; an individual outside the mind cannot. If instead the claim is that the essence, as it exists mentally, would be a substance if it existed outside the mind, then the image is an accident of the soul. If it existed outside, it would still be a quality of the soul, not a substance or any other outside category. If the claim is that this essence exists in the mind in such a way that, under an impossible assumption, it could become another essence outside the mind, that claim adds nothing. The same could be said of any essence in any kind of existence. We could say: if a substance were an accident, it would exist in a subject; if a body were an intellect, it would have every perfection; if a possible thing were necessary, it would create the world.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00854

This view also leaves no real difference between mental forms and mere likenesses or shadows. A mental image would be like a picture painted on a wall: it would count as a person, horse, elephant, trees, or rivers only because, if it existed outside the mind, it would be those things. But it could never exist outside that surface. The truth is that the intellectual images of substances outside the mind are the real meanings and realities of those things. A substance, or a body, has a meaning and a sensible image. Its sensible image is the substance as sensed; its intellectual image is the meaning of substance, understood by the intellect as existing on its own. The intellect understands this without needing another image to be present in the intellect. The same applies to the idea of an animal: it includes the understood meanings of body, life, and sensation. These meanings do not have to be separate existences.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00855

Nor is the intellectual meaning something that exists in a subject that could do without it. This is a higher, more complete kind of existence. All these meanings can be said of one body as what it is, even though that body exists in a position and direction and none of the intellectual images has a position or direction. It is even more fitting to say that these meanings are one with an intellectual reality. One understood meaning being one with another in intellectual existence is more fitting than an understood meaning being one with something sensed and one with it in sensory existence. Avicenna himself, at the start of the fourth section of The Pointers, says that the understood animal exists in the sensed animal. The animal understood as a general kind clearly has an existence that cannot be pointed to or located in space. Yet it is connected to, and one in meaning with, the animal we sense. This does not mean that the intellectual image is an accident in each individual animal. It is more truly a substance and more independent than these lowly, changing, generated and decaying animals. The same applies to other understood images of substances and other kinds.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00856

People fall into these problems because they think that intellectual images exist in the soul in the same way accidents exist in what contains them. They also reject the claim that the knower and the known can be one. So they cannot escape the problem of how the mind could know a substance without making knowledge both a substance and an accident. Their best answer is that “accident” is an incidental feature when said of a substance, and that substance and accident do not conflict in mental existence, only in outside existence. They say that the nature of a substance remains the same even when it needs the mind as a subject in order to exist there. It can still be called a substance because outside the mind it does not depend on a subject. It would be wrong to say that one thing is both a substance and an accident in the same kind of existence. But, they argue, having the essence of a substance in the mind does not require this.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00857

This answer also fails. First, being an accident means having the kind of existence that depends on a subject. That is what it means for something to exist in a subject. Existing in a subject is the way qualities such as blackness and heat exist. As we explained earlier, existence does not truly attach itself to an essence as another feature that can come and go. The mind separates them in its analysis. So being an accident is not like an added feature that may change while the essence remains. If a substance such as a human being had the same kind of existence as an accident—that is, if its very being were to exist in a subject—it could not lose that existence and take on another while remaining the same essence. Comparing the way existence belongs to an essence with the way other incidental features belong to it is a comparison without a real likeness. A thing's existence is not truly an added feature. It is the thing's being real, outside the mind or in it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00858

Even if we allowed that one thing could be a substance in its nature and an accident in the mind, the problem would remain. They agree that knowledge of each category belongs to that category, while they also say that all knowledge is a quality of the soul. So when we know a substance, knowledge would have to be both a substance and a quality. This is not answered by Avicenna’s reply. Saying that being an accident is not essential to what is beneath it may allow a thing to be a substance outside the mind and an accident inside it. But this does not work for the highest categories, because they are essential to the kinds and individual things beneath them. An essential feature cannot change across different kinds of existence without ceasing to be essential. Then it would no longer be true that the same essence exists in another way in the mind.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00859

A careful thinker asks how one thing could be both a substance and a quality for someone who already rejects its being both a substance and an accident. The conflict between substance and quality seems to come from one existing in a subject and the other not. But not depending on a subject is also true of a substance and a quality, so why does that cause a problem for one and not the other?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00860

Someone might answer that, just as substance means an essence that exists independently outside the mind, quality means an essence that exists as an accident, that is, without parts and without a relation between parts. The same would apply to quantity and the other categories. But this brings back the earlier problem: it would leave no part of the essences or meanings of things that remained the same in mental and outside existence. It also follows from their view that the substantial image of a thing in the mind is an individual image present in one particular mind. Whatever exists in one particular mind must be a particular thing in the outside world. So the intellectual image of the essence of a substance would exist outside the mind as a quality. It would then be both a substance and a quality in outside existence, which is clearly impossible. They have no way out except to say that an essence exists in the mind, but that “outside existence” means an existence in which the features of that essence take effect. Blackness outside the mind makes the eyes contract; heat outside the mind warms things. When these images exist in the mind, those effects do not occur. So they call the first outside existence and the second mental existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00861
But the problem remains. We now turn to the view we have already pointed toward and will make the case for it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00862
VII. What It Means for the Intellect to Become One with What It Understands
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00863

The question of how the soul understands the forms of things is one of the hardest questions in philosophy. No Muslim philosopher, as far as we know, had fully worked it out. We saw how difficult it is to explain how knowing a substance could itself be a substance and an accident. We found no answer in the major books of the leading philosopher, Avicenna—The Healing, The Salvation, The Pointers, or The Sources of Wisdom—that could resolve the problem. Avicenna’s followers, including his student Bahmanyār, the distinguished commentator Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi, and later thinkers, offered nothing we could rely on either. If even these respected scholars could not settle it, what can we expect from those who trade in guesses, fantasies, and endless disputes?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00864

So we turned to the One who brings all things about, asking for help with this difficult question. We had often seen Him guide those seeking knowledge, reveal divine truths to those who need them, and spread the light of guidance. As I was writing this chapter, He opened a new door of knowledge for me and made a clear way into the matter. That is a gift from God, given to whomever He wills. In gratitude, I will now share it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00865

Images of things are of two kinds. A material image depends on matter, position, place, and other such conditions. In that material mode of existence, it cannot be an object of thought in act; it cannot even be sensed in that same way except indirectly. The other kind is free of matter, position, and place. If it is wholly free of them, it is an object of thought in act; if it is free only in part, it is imagined or sensed.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00866

All philosophers agree that an image actually understood has one and the same existence in itself and for the intellect that understands it. The same is true of something actually sensed: its existence as a sensed thing and its existence for the sensing subject are one in the same respect. If an actually understood image had an existence separate from the intellect, then the two would be distinct beings, like blackness and the body in which it occurs. Each would have to be able to exist without the other. But that is not how an actual object of thought exists.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00867

An actual object of thought has no existence apart from the existence in which it is understood. It is intelligible in itself, not because something else turns it into an object of thought. If its intellect were separate from it, then, considered on its own, it would not be intelligible. Its existence would not be the intellectual existence of an understood form. But an essence free of matter is intelligible in act, whether or not some outside intellect happens to understand it. This is unlike a body's being in motion: if we set aside what moves it, it is no longer moving in that respect, only a body. It is also unlike a body's being hot: without what heats it, it is no longer hot, because the body's existence is not the same as the existence of heat.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00868

The case of an actual object of thought is different. It cannot exist in act without being intelligible in act. Its very existence is its being understood, whether or not another intellect understands it. So it is an intellect in act as well as an object of thought in act. Otherwise, the intellect and the intelligible would come apart, even though each is in act. As we have already explained, the intellect and what it understands must match one another in existence and in level: if one is actual, the other is actual; if one is only potential, the other is only potential; and if one exists at a certain level, the other exists at that level too.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00869

The same applies to sensible forms. Something may be sensible only in possibility, or it may be sensed in act. What is sensed in act shares its existence with the sensing substance in act. Sensation does not happen by the sense removing the very same form from its matter, as many philosophers have thought, while imagination removes it still further. A form impressed in matter cannot move with its own identity from one piece of matter to another.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00870

Nor does sensation mean that a sense power moves toward a form of the sensed thing that remains in its matter, as some have said about sight. Nor is sensation merely the soul's relation to those material forms, as the author of The Book of Lights says. A spatial relation to a body is not perception, and a knowing relation cannot be formed with things that have position and matter. Sensation occurs when the Giver causes a luminous, perceptive form to appear. Through it, awareness takes place. That form is the sense faculty in act and the sensed thing in act. Before it appears, both exist only in possibility. The form in a particular material thing prepares the way for this new form to flow from the Giver. The account of how one image can be sense, sensing subject, and sensed thing is like the account of how one intellectual image can be intellect, intellecting subject, and intelligible.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00871

The First Teacher says in The Theology of Aristotle: “Sight does not reach things outside itself until it becomes, in a way, those things. Then it senses and knows them truly, according to its capacity. The same is true of the intellect: when it looks at intellectual things, it does not reach them until it and they become one. Sight looks at what is outside things, while intellect looks at what is within them. Its union with them takes different forms, and with some it is stronger than the union of the senses with what they sense. The longer ordinary sight looks at a thing, the more it is harmed, until the thing falls outside its sight and it sees nothing. Intellectual sight is the opposite.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00872

What we have said answers many objections to the claim that forms with different natures are imprinted in the intellect. It also answers objections to the claim that possible things are imprinted in God's being, as many followers of the school of Aristotle hold. If understanding happened by images being imprinted in the knower, then when the soul understood substance, quantity, and other kinds of thing, one and the same thing would belong to two basic categories. And God's being would have to serve as a place for possible things. These and other serious problems are discussed elsewhere.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00873

Some people say that the human soul, which is an intellect only in possibility, meets intellectual forms and understands them. But what enables this receptive power to understand a form? Does it understand the form by its bare self, before any intellectual images are present? How could an unknowing, unlit, ordinary self understand a form that is bright in itself and purely intelligible? A blind eye cannot see. If the soul understands the form through another intellectual image that lights it up, then that image is itself an intellect in act, just as it is an intelligible in act. No further image is needed; otherwise the same question would arise again without end. So the intellect and what it understands are one, without any difference in their existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00874

Someone might reply that this image is only a means by which the soul understands other things, while the soul understands the image itself directly. But unless the image were first understood, it could not help the soul understand anything else. It does not work like a tool used in physical labor. It is more like light in seeing: we see the light first, and through it we see other things. We have also proved that an intellectual image is intelligible in itself, whether or not anything else understands it. The same is true of something actually sensed: in the existence in which it is sensed, it is sensed in act, even if we set aside everything else.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00875

An image that lets the soul understand does not exist in the soul as a house, wealth, or children exist for their owner. Those things are connected to a person only by a relation; their presence does not complete or develop that person. A natural bodily form does complete matter and make it an actual thing. Matter is not any definite thing until a form gives it shape. The form does not arrive as a separate being moving into matter; rather, matter rises from a less complete state to a more complete one. The soul likewise becomes intellect in act after being intellect only in possibility. An intellectual image does not attach to the soul as a separate thing, like a horse standing beside us, or like an accident added to a substance that could exist without it. Such connections amount only to relations; they do not complete anything. By contrast, an image that the soul understands completes it more deeply than natural forms complete matter.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00876
VIII. Confirming That the Intellect and What It Understands Become One
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00877

Avicenna states in many of his books that the intellect and what it understands cannot become one. He strongly rejects this idea and treats it as absurd. In this chapter I will present his arguments against it and the objections he raises against those who say that intellect and knower become one. Then I will answer them.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00878

In The Pointers, Avicenna says that some prominent thinkers believe that when an intellecting substance understands an intellectual form, it becomes that form. Suppose, he says, that an intellecting substance understands A and, as these thinkers claim, becomes the very A it understands. Is it still what it was before it understood A, or has something in it ceased to be what it was? If nothing changed, then it makes no difference whether it understands A. If something in it ceased to be, that change must either be a state added to it while its substance remains, like any other change—and then the claim is false—or it must be its very substance. In that case its substance has disappeared and something else has appeared; it has not become another thing while remaining itself. If you think this through, Avicenna adds, the view also requires a shared matter and a composite change, not a simple one.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00879

He makes the same point in another passage: if the intellect first understands A and then B, does it remain as it was when it understood A, whether or not it understands B? Or does it become something else? Either way, the earlier problem returns. He also mocks the book Porphyry wrote about intellect and intelligible forms. The philosophers in Aristotle’s school praise it, he says, even though neither they nor Porphyry himself understood it. One of Porphyry's contemporaries contradicted him, and Porphyry's reply was even weaker. Avicenna then gives a general argument against any two things becoming one: if both remain, they are two distinct things; if one no longer exists, the thing that existed has disappeared. He calls the idea that one thing could remain itself and yet become another, without changing or combining with something else, poetic and unintelligible.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00880

In The Healing, Avicenna repeats the argument. If the soul became the intelligible forms, he says, it would have to give up one form and take on another. Then the first thing would have disappeared, while only its subject or a part of it remained. If that is not what happens, we must explain how it happens. When something becomes something else, is it then present or absent? If it is present and the other thing is also present, there are two things, not one. If it is absent, then the present thing has become something absent, not another existing thing. If the first thing disappeared, it did not become something else; it simply ceased to exist and something else appeared. How, then, could the soul become the forms of things?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00881

Avicenna says that Porphyry's Isagoge is the best-known example of this view, but that its language is imaginative and poetic rather than clear. The images of things settle in and adorn the soul, making it a kind of place for them by means of the material intellect. If the soul itself became an actual form, and that form were fully actual with no potentiality to receive anything else, the soul could not accept another form. Yet we see that it does. If the new form did not differ from the first, the soul would somehow both accept and not accept the same thing. If it did differ, the soul would have become something other than itself. Avicenna concludes that the soul is the knower, while “intellect” means either its power to understand or the forms it understands. Since the forms are understood in the soul, intellect, knower, and intelligible cannot be one in us. He allows that they may be one in another being, a point he says he will discuss later. He adds that if “material intellect” means the soul's general capacity to understand, it remains in us as long as we live in a body; if it means a capacity for one particular thing, that capacity disappears when it becomes actual.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00882

Before answering Avicenna, we must keep two things in mind. First, existence is what makes a thing real and individual, and it is the source of what that thing is. Existence can grow stronger or weaker, become more complete or less complete, while the individual remains itself. A human being passes through many stages, from embryo to child to adult who understands and is understood, while its individual existence continues.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00883

Second, there are three different senses in which things might be said to become one. The first is when two existing things merge so that their two existences become one. Avicenna is right that this is impossible. The second is when one concept or essence becomes identical in meaning with another, so that each can be substituted for the other in a definition. That too is impossible: different meanings cannot become one meaning. The concept of the knower cannot become the concept of the intelligible. But one simple existence can truthfully be called both knower and intelligible, with different meanings that do not divide that existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00884

The third sense is this: something develops so that a concept or universal nature that could not previously be said of it can now truly be said of it. This is not impossible; it happens. A human being contains, in one individual, the meanings found separately in nonliving things, plants, animals, and intellect. Someone might say that these meanings are present in a human because the person has many different powers, not because of one power. I reply that they belong to the person's own form, which includes those powers. All human powers of perception and action flow from one simple source: the soul, the person's true self. Those powers are branches of that one source, which senses through the senses and acts through the limbs.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00885

In the same way, the simple intellect that philosophers speak of is the source of the many distinct things understood by the mind. Later in this book it will become clear that the Active Intellect in us is all existing things in this sense: its own being is what makes it true to say all the universal meanings found in the forms of things in the world. It is not strange for one existence to develop until a meaning that could not earlier be said of it can now be said of it. As the saying goes, it is no wonder that God gathers the whole world into one.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00886

With these points in place, we can answer Avicenna. His general argument in The Pointers says that if both things exist, they remain two distinct things. We do not accept that. Many different meanings can exist in one existence. “Animal” and “rational” are different meanings, either of which can be considered apart from the other, yet both exist in one human being.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00887

Avicenna's general argument in The Healing says that when one thing becomes another, the first must either exist or not exist. If both exist, they are two; if the first does not, it has disappeared. We reply that both meanings can exist in one existence. There is no contradiction in many different meanings being present in one being. Otherwise, how could the human soul be one simple substance that is knowing, able, active, hearing, seeing, and alive? And how could the one divine being be the source of every perfection and every good name in one simple existence, with no different parts or sides?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00888

Now consider Avicenna's arguments about the knower and the intelligible. In The Pointers he asks whether the knower remains what it was before it understood A. We answer: it remains itself, except that what was incomplete or lacking in it is gone. The change is like a child becoming an adult. The child loses nothing substantial or positive; what falls away is only a lack, such as being immature or still only capable of adulthood.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00889

Avicenna himself explains two ways in which one thing can come from another. In the first, the first thing naturally moves toward completion in the second. A child is a child because it is on its way to adulthood. When it becomes an adult, it has not been destroyed; it has been completed. It has lost no essential or accidental feature except what belonged to its earlier weakness and potential. In the second way, a thing is not naturally moving toward the next form, even though the matter that carries it can receive that form. Water becomes air by losing its watery form and taking on an airy form. In the first case, the first thing itself remains in the second and becomes complete. In the second, only part of the first remains; its earlier substance is destroyed. Avicenna's own account therefore allows a thing to become another while remaining itself, when it develops toward its natural completion.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00890

When Avicenna says that the soul would be the same whether or not it understood A, we answer that this would follow only if the soul did not itself become the source of a perfection that it lacked before. It is surprising that he denies this, since he says that the human soul develops from potentiality in every kind of perception, including sensation and imagination, until it becomes intellect in act and understands most—or even all—intelligible things, as the simple intellect does. Yet on his account, nothing that could not be said of a soul at the beginning can later be said of it in itself. That would make the souls of prophets, children, people with severe mental disabilities, and embryos all equal in their essential nature; their only differences would be accidental features attached to existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00891

Of course, these perfections differ in meaning from the human essence. But the difference between existence and essence is a difference in our way of thinking, not a split in reality. Existence is what makes things real; essence follows it. When Avicenna says that if the soul changes, something must have disappeared while the soul remains as a subject, we answer that no part of its nature or existence disappears. Only a lack falls away. The soul was less complete and becomes stronger in its way of existing. This is unlike ordinary changes in which one positive feature gives way to its opposite, as when water becomes air or something cold becomes hot.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00892

Avicenna's further claim—that the soul must disappear and a different thing must appear if its very self changes—is also answered by the difference between existence and meaning. What disappears is only a lack, such as potentiality. A thing can also change gradually in its very substance, without its existence ending and a separate thing taking its place. Consider heat that grows stronger. If each moment of stronger heat were a separate existence, motion would be made of indivisible instants and separate pieces of distance. We have already shown that this is impossible. The growing heat has one continuous existence, even though it has different degrees of heat at different parts of the duration of its change. These degrees are distinct in meaning but belong to one continuous existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00893

So it is not impossible for different meanings to be present in one existence, as they are when they are drawn from many separate things. What is impossible is for one actual heat to become another actual heat as a second separate thing, or for two fully existing beings to become one being. Every actual existence has its own definite identity; one identity cannot become another. Every essence has its own definition and meaning; the meaning of a human being cannot become the meaning of a horse. But reason does not rule out every case in which different meanings belong to one existence. Proof rules out only certain combinations, such as the Necessary and the possible, potentiality and actuality, substance and accident, opposites, and other pairs that cannot share one existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00894

When Avicenna says that such a change requires shared matter, we do not deny that a thing changing toward completion may depend in some way on a material substance that is itself in motion. But if he means that the thing is externally composite in itself, we do not accept that. A form's existence is not made of parts, especially when it is ready to become intellect in act. If he means that a living human being is made up of soul and bodily matter, we accept that, but it does not refute our point.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00895

Avicenna's other argument in The Healing concerns how the soul could already be a form and still be able to receive further forms. We answer that when the soul first came to be in the body's matter, it was the form of a bodily thing. At the beginning, it was like a sensory or imagined form, not yet an intellectual form. A purely intellectual form and bodily matter could not make one bodily kind, such as a human being, without the matter first passing through stages of development and change. The soul at the beginning of life was one form among the beings of this world, but it had the capacity to rise gradually toward the spiritual world. It was first the form of a bodily being, with the potential to receive intellectual forms.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00896

The soul's sensory form is like matter for its imagined form, and the imagined form is like matter for the intellectual forms. First, the earliest intelligible meanings flow into it; then, gradually, the later ones. That is how the soul becomes those forms. Avicenna says that a form itself cannot contain the potential to receive another form. We do not accept this. The capacity to develop is included in the form, as a distinguishing feature is included in a simple kind.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00897

Avicenna says that the capacity to receive belongs only to what receives the form. We agree, but “receiving” has more than one meaning. It can mean undergoing change when an opposite form appears, as when something continuous becomes separate or water becomes air. Or it can mean having the capacity to develop toward greater completeness. A form can have this second kind of capacity as it becomes more complete.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00898

In short, potentiality may be joined to a thing's absence in the outside world, or to an absence that exists only in thought. The first belongs to receptive matter; the second belongs to a form connected to matter. A form wholly free of matter in every respect has no further perfection waiting for it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00899

Avicenna says that if the next form does not differ from the first, then receiving and not receiving are the same. We answer that the next form is not a second actual form added to the first. It is a meaning united with the soul in one existence. By “the form of a thing,” we mean its existence, not a general idea of it. Each thing has one simple form, but that form can make many perfections real. It may have a strong, complete existence or a weak, incomplete one.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00900

As the soul grows stronger, it becomes the source of many meanings. Each meaning, if it existed separately, might be the form of an incomplete bodily kind: an understood horse, tree, or piece of earth. When these meanings exist in bodily matter outside the mind, each is the form of a material kind. When understood in the intellectual world, each is joined to an intellectual substance. It need not be the whole nature of that substance or its intellectual mode of existence. It can be one of the meanings united with it, in a way higher and more complete than its union with lowly bodily forms. Intellectual existence is a higher, nobler existence, in which all intelligible things can be present together in one existence, unlike the numerical unity of bodies.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00901

When Avicenna says that if the soul differs from the form it has become something other than itself, we answer that it has not become numerically different. It has changed in completeness, or in the meaning we can truly apply to it, while the same existence remains and becomes more noble.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00902

He also says that the soul is the knower, while intellect means either the soul's power to understand or the forms it understands. We have already shown that the first meaning cannot be intellect in act. Whether we mean the soul's capacity or its bare self, before intellectual forms are present, it cannot be exactly the same as intellect in act. Otherwise, the same thing would be potential and actual, ignorant and knowing. As for the second meaning—that the understood forms are intellect in act while the soul, which is the bodily animal's perfection, understands them—we have shown why this account fails from both sides.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00903

First, from the soul's side: how could a soul bare of intellect understand intellectual forms that are separate from it in their existence? A thing can be truly said to have something only if the thing exists in the same setting where the feature is said of it. If the thing is absent in that setting, no other thing can truly belong to it there. What exists belongs to what exists, not to what is absent. The same rule applies to intellectual existence: a purely intellectual form, free of matter and its ties, can be present to something only if that thing also has intellectual existence. An actual object of thought can belong only to something that is itself an actual intellect. So before the soul becomes an intellect, it cannot have an intellectual image in itself, except potentially, as imagined or sensed forms exist before the light of the Active Intellect shines on them.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00904

Now consider the intellectual forms themselves. By a proof God inspired in me, I have shown that each form is intelligible in its own being, apart from everything else. Whether or not something exists to understand it, it is intelligible in itself. If it is intelligible apart from the soul, then it is an intellect in itself. The soul must therefore become one with it. That is the very point we are making.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-00905

Although Avicenna strongly rejects the union of knower and intelligible in his other books, he sets out this very idea in The Beginning and the Return. There he argues that the Necessary Being understands Himself and is intellect and intelligible. I do not know whether he presents this only as another school's view, because of the purpose of that book, or whether it was his own belief after the light of truth appeared to him. Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi, in his commentary on The Pointers, excuses Avicenna by saying that The Beginning and the Return was written to explain the view held by Aristotle’s followers, as Avicenna says at the start. From this we can see that only the earliest philosophers had fully understood this noble teaching. Later scholars of debate and argument did not inherit it—until God granted it to a poor seeker and opened his heart through His power.
